detail.extracted_title: From London’s Here East to Oman’s Archives: Putting National Memory to Work in the Creative Economy
detail.excerpt: Inspired by His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tariq’s visit to London’s Here East innovation campus, creative economy researcher Azzan bin Khamis Al Subhi maps a practical blueprint for connecting Omani archives, universities, and creative enterprises into lasting cultural production.
detail.article_html:
When His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tariq toured London’s Here East innovation and technology campus on October 22, 2026—meeting chief executives and examining ventures across clean energy, space, defense, and advanced engineering—the visit highlighted a distinctive institutional architecture. Built by repurposing the press and broadcast centers from the 2012 London Olympics, Here East places deep-tech incubators like Plexal and University College London spinouts such as Panda Surgical under the same roof as heritage labs, museum collections, and performing arts studios.

Writing in Oman Daily, creative economy researcher Azzan bin Khamis Al Subhi asks what that convergence of scholarship, preserved memory, and enterprise could unlock inside the Sultanate: how can Oman build shared institutional workflows where historical records spark new creative products, skilled professions, and self-sustaining small businesses?

Where Archives Sit Beside Makers and Engineers

Inside Here East, cultural memory operates as an active creative partner rather than a closed vault. In May 2025, the Victoria and Albert Museum opened V&A East Storehouse inside the complex, giving researchers, designers, and makers organized public access to more than 1,000 archival collections spanning art, design, theatre, and performance through direct catalog requests and study appointments. Nearby, UCL’s campus space houses its Institute for Sustainable Heritage alongside architecture, engineering, computer science, and rapid-prototyping labs—bringing archival verification and contemporary product design into the same conversation from day one.

Even artificial intelligence enters that creative loop when clear boundaries are respected. Studio Wayne McGregor, another Here East resident, collaborated with Google Arts & Culture on its Living Archive project, drawing on a 25-year choreographic archive and 100 hours of recorded movement to train an AI creative tool used in staging a 2019 performance.

Governmental and historical manuscripts naturally demand stricter stewardship than a private dance archive. Still, Al Subhi notes that documented memory can supply authentic raw material and digital tools can surface fresh patterns, provided audiences can always distinguish between the original historical document, scholarly interpretation, and artistic treatment—preserving historical integrity regardless of how sophisticated the visual presentation becomes.

Two-Way Knowledge Transfer and Oman Vision 2040

Linking cultural heritage to enterprise aligns directly with Oman’s broader economic diversification drive. At the 2026 Together We Progress Forum, His Highness Sayyid Theyazin bin Haitham Al Said, Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs, outlined his office’s mandate to track diversification programs and coordinate public economic policy across institutions. Speaking in London on October 21, 2026, during the 50th anniversary of the Anglo-Omani Society, His Highness also pointed to the Smart Industries Initiative as a two-way platform for research-backed technology transfer between British and Omani industries.

Applying that same two-way principle to the creative industries, Al Subhi suggests pairing Omani archivists, designers, and software developers with international specialists through joint residencies and co-production projects built around rights-cleared heritage materials. Oman enters any such partnership from a position of cultural depth—bringing centuries of manuscripts, maritime records, and contextual scholarship—while ensuring every completed project transfers full documentation, software maintenance tools, and operational know-how to Omani teams.

A One-Year Omani Pilot From Document to Market

Rather than starting with new concrete buildings, Al Subhi proposes testing the model through a focused one-year pilot anchored in Oman’s existing institutions. Under clear governance, the National Records and Archives Authority would select rights-cleared materials and establish historical context; Omani universities would contribute applied verification and student training during production; creative small and medium enterprises and freelancers would design and market the finished experiences; and schools, museums, and cultural or tourism operators would act as genuine “first buyers” commissioning solutions for real visitor or classroom needs.

Consider a single governorate’s documented history of traditional crafts and historic souqs. Working from verified photographs, manuscripts, and oral accounts, a multidisciplinary team of historians, designers, and coders could produce an interactive site installation for a local heritage monument, a curriculum kit for schools, and visual storytelling assets for regional artisans—testing audience response before agreeing on licensing and service fees.

Clear intellectual property rules, strict source attribution for any AI-assisted tools, community participation from the earliest planning stages, and fair professional compensation for memory-holders keep that ecosystem grounded in trust. Aligned with Oman Vision 2040’s commitment to sustainable investment in heritage, culture, and the arts, turning an archival record into the starting point of contemporary Omani enterprise honors the past while giving young talent practical tools to shape the future.

detail.instagram_caption:
His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tariq's October 22, 2026 visit to London's Here East innovation campus—built inside the repurposed 2012 Olympic press and broadcast centers—offered a close look at an ecosystem where deep-tech startups, university labs, and living museum archives share the same creative floor. Inside the complex, V&A East Storehouse opened more than 1,000 archival collections to researchers and designers in May 2025 alongside UCL's Institute for Sustainable Heritage.

Creative economy researcher Azzan bin Khamis Al Subhi explores how Oman can adapt that institutional workflow to put national memory to work under Oman Vision 2040, echoing His Highness Sayyid Theyazin bin Haitham Al Said's call for two-way knowledge transfer through the Smart Industries Initiative.

Rather than starting with new buildings, Al Subhi proposes a focused one-year Omani pilot connecting the National Records and Archives Authority, local universities, creative SMEs, and cultural or educational first buyers—transforming verified manuscripts, photographs, and craft histories into interactive heritage experiences, school kits, and commercial design while protecting historical accuracy, intellectual property, and fair returns for memory-holders.

Read the full story at omanspire.om (link in bio).
